article_title: Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling
citation: Hooshyar, D.; Šír, G.; Yang, Y.; Kärkkäinen, T.; Hämäläinen, R.; Krivich, E.; Cukurova, M.; Gašević, D.; Azevedo, R. (2026). Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08263
title: PyNeuraLogic framework for lifted relational neural-symbolic learning
description: PyNeuraLogic implements the Lifted Relational Neural Networks paradigm, expressing data as logical predicates and model architectures as parameterized weighted logical rule templates that are grounded into differentiable computation graphs. The article states it "elevates neural-symbolic learning to the relational level, utilizing differentiable first-order logic programming". Because temporal sequences are a linear case of relational graphs, it can subsume RNN and graph architectures while enforcing explicit symbolic rules. The framework is released at the printed GitHub URL and is used here to implement Responsible-DKT.
requirements: Data expressed as logical ground facts and a declared rule template; grounding against available facts to unroll the computation graph before backpropagation
constraints: Propositional-level neural-symbolic models it supersedes struggle with structured or dynamically sized data; the framework's scope is relational, differentiable logic programming
target_learners: Researchers and developers of learner-modelling systems
target_learning_goals: Sequential learner knowledge modelling with injected symbolic educational knowledge
examples: Responsible-DKT was implemented as a single neural-symbolic template in PyNeuraLogic, grounded per student against interaction facts
key_sources: Hooshyar, D.; Šír, G.; Yang, Y.; Kärkkäinen, T.; Hämäläinen, R.; Krivich, E.; Cukurova, M.; Gašević, D.; Azevedo, R. (2026). Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08263

article_title: Simulating Novice Students Using Machine Unlearning and Relearning in Large Language Models
citation: Jiajia Song, Zhihan Guo, and Jionghao Lin. (2026). Simulating Novice Students Using Machine Unlearning and Relearning in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26142
title: Python MCQ dataset for unlearning and relearning experiments
description: A dataset of Python multiple-choice questions built from web-collected items (Sanfoundry, GeeksforGeeks, PyNative) plus LLM-generated items generated with ChatGPT-5.1 to balance concept coverage. The article states "The dataset contains 2,074 MCQs spanning 22 concept categories, combining web-collected questions with LLM-generated items to broaden coverage and increase diversity." Each question carries a description, options, correct answer, concept label, and explanation, with metadata retained for source traceability.
requirements: Basic validity screening, including checks for option completeness and answer consistency
constraints: Coverage across web-collected concepts is uneven, and some categories include repetitive question styles or limited variation in phrasing
target_learners: LLM-based teachable agents simulating novice students
target_learning_goals: Python programming concepts such as Functions, Operators, Data Types, and Lists
examples: KC-level splitting ranked concepts by question count, with the top 70% (16 KCs, 1,823 questions) forming the unlearning target set
key_sources: Jiajia Song, Zhihan Guo, and Jionghao Lin. (2026). Simulating Novice Students Using Machine Unlearning and Relearning in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26142

article_title: Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding
citation: Ishari Amarasinghe; Davinia Hernández-Leo; H. Ulrich Hoppe (2021). Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09351-9
title: PyramidApp with teacher-facing mirroring and guiding dashboard
description: PyramidApp is a web-based tool implementing a version of the Pyramid collaborative script, providing "an activity authoring space and a teacher-facing LA dashboard for teachers as well as an activity enactment space for students". Teachers configure class size, group size, pyramid levels, durations, and up to 10 expected keywords, and can enable automatic alerts. The dashboard has Responses Related and Participation Related tabs, a timeline with remaining-time countdown, runtime controls (increase time, pause, next level, end), and supporting posting predefined messages to groups. The guiding support adds an alert mechanism flagging critical moments such as missing keywords, skipped submissions, and insufficient remaining submission or voting time.
requirements: Teachers trained beforehand on the dashboard features and functionalities; the article reports around 45 minutes to one hour of training per teacher
constraints: Alert criteria were fixed by the system; one teacher suggested alert thresholds such as the half-of-time rule should be a parameter modifiable by the teacher for activities with longer discussion and rating times
target_learners: higher-education students working in classroom collaborative learning sessions
target_learning_goals: structured consensus-building discussion across individual, small-group, and class-wide social planes
examples: Alerts included no keywords detected within the first 20% of answers, and more-time-for-voting when 50% of groups had not finished voting and 50% of voting time had passed
key_sources: Ishari Amarasinghe; Davinia Hernández-Leo; H. Ulrich Hoppe (2021). Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09351-9

article_title: Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding
citation: Ishari Amarasinghe; Davinia Hernández-Leo; H. Ulrich Hoppe (2021). Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09351-9
title: Pyramid collaborative learning flow pattern
description: The Pyramid script structures collaborative learning flow so students first solve a problem individually, then join small groups (usually pairs) to share and agree on common solutions via voting and chat, and are progressively merged into increasingly larger groups forming the pyramid structure. It "aims to provide opportunities for all learners to express their solutions and to discuss their ideas with peers" and to support consensus-building across phases one after another. In this study it was enacted with PyramidApp in classrooms with teacher orchestration support.
requirements: Sustained participation from all learners from beginning to end of the consensus-building process; teacher monitoring so groups reaching premature or misleading consensus can be redirected
constraints: Groups advance at different rates, creating idle time for faster groups and potential off-task behaviour, while slower groups need more time; teachers cannot constantly distribute attention across social planes without support
target_learners: classroom learners from individual through pair to large-group phases
target_learning_goals: reaching informed consensus and expressing and discussing ideas with peers
examples: Sessions in the study ranged from 6 to 20 minutes with 7 to 71 students, e.g. a question about sharing knowledge about research writing
key_sources: Ishari Amarasinghe; Davinia Hernández-Leo; H. Ulrich Hoppe (2021). Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09351-9

article_title: Mediators that matter: Psychological distress, developmental assets, and educational outcomes among Black youth.
citation: Rose, T., Joe, S., & Hancock, G. R. (2024). Mediators that Matter: Psychological Distress, Developmental Assets, and Educational Outcomes among Black Youth. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000876
title: Positive youth development theory and the developmental asset framework as an asset-based lens on Black adolescent educational outcomes
description: The study is guided by positive youth development theory (PYDT), under which "adolescents are seen as “co-producers” of their development, as they are influenced by and influence their contexts". Building on PYDT, the Search Institute's developmental asset framework treats assets as "opportunities, experiences, and supports" that serve protective or promotive functions. The authors apply this asset-based lens to challenge deficit-based narratives about Black students, focusing on internal assets — positive identity (self-esteem, mastery) and commitment to learning (school bonding, aspirations, expectations) — as mediators between psychological distress and educational outcomes.
requirements: Assets are described as malleable, making them suitable targets for individual- or group-level, particularly school-level, interventions
constraints: The study examined only a limited set of internal assets, some with varied reliability, using cross-sectional secondary data
target_learners: Black adolescents ages 13–17 (African American and Caribbean Black)
target_learning_goals: Educational outcomes including grades, grade repetition, suspensions, and expulsions
examples: The study modeled five assets (self-esteem, mastery, school bonding, educational aspirations, educational expectations) as mediators in path analyses of NSAL-A data
key_sources: Rose, T., Joe, S., & Hancock, G. R. (2024). Mediators that Matter: Psychological Distress, Developmental Assets, and Educational Outcomes among Black Youth. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000876

article_title: Evaluation of Parsons Problems with Menu-Based Self-Explanation Prompts in a Mobile Python Tutor
citation: Fabic, G. V. F., Mitrovic, A., & Neshatian, K. (2019). Evaluation of Parsons Problems with Menu-Based Self-Explanation Prompts in a Mobile Python Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 29, 507–535. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00184-0
title: PyKinetic: a mobile Python tutor with Parsons problems with incomplete LOCs and menu-based SE prompts
description: PyKinetic is "a mobile tutor developed using Android SDK to teach Python 3.x programming", designed for novices as a complement to traditional lectures. It presents Parsons problems whose lines of code (LOCs) are randomly ordered with correct indentation; learners drag and drop LOCs and complete incomplete LOCs by selecting from menu options instead of typing. The study version contained 15 Parsons problems across six Python topics, with 22 menu-based SE prompts (14 conceptual, 8 procedural) given after solving incomplete LOCs. The experimental version added SE prompts; the control version was identical apart from the SE prompts.
requirements: Learners use Android devices (version 4.0 and higher); problems are presented in portrait mode, a change made after the pilot study
constraints: Problems limited to a maximum of 16 LOCs; a maximum of 3 incomplete LOCs per problem; SE prompts cannot be skipped and allow only a single attempt
target_learning_goals: code writing and code execution (procedural knowledge)
examples: In the evaluation study, 63 participants from two universities used PyKinetic for about an hour between a 15-min pre-test and 15-min post-test
key_sources: Fabic, G. V. F., Mitrovic, A., & Neshatian, K. (2019). Evaluation of Parsons Problems with Menu-Based Self-Explanation Prompts in a Mobile Python Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 29, 507–535. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00184-0

article_title: Evaluation of Parsons Problems with Menu-Based Self-Explanation Prompts in a Mobile Python Tutor
citation: Fabic, G. V. F., Mitrovic, A., & Neshatian, K. (2019). Evaluation of Parsons Problems with Menu-Based Self-Explanation Prompts in a Mobile Python Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 29, 507–535. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00184-0
title: Parsons problems design for smartphones: single combined area, pre-indented single LOCs, incomplete LOCs with menu-based SE prompts
description: The article's Parsons problems differ from common implementations in four ways the authors enumerate. First, students solve problems "in the same area where the LOCs are presented", with no separation between problem and solution space, making better use of limited smartphone screen space. Second, all lines are provided with correct indentation as scaffolding for novices. Third, all blocks contain only single LOCs, encouraging students to think about each individual line. Fourth, the problems contain incomplete LOCs accompanied by menu-based SE prompts that learners must answer upon solving them, targeting both procedural and conceptual knowledge.
requirements: Menu-based SE prompts require feedback on incorrect choices so learners with misconceptions receive guidance
constraints: Combining problem and solution areas might overwhelm learners because all LOCs are displayed at once, though the authors did not observe this as an issue given the 16-LOC limit
examples: The study version contained 15 Parsons problems across six Python topics, given in a fixed order of increasing difficulty, with 22 SE prompts
key_sources: Fabic, G. V. F., Mitrovic, A., & Neshatian, K. (2019). Evaluation of Parsons Problems with Menu-Based Self-Explanation Prompts in a Mobile Python Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 29, 507–535. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00184-0

article_title: Effects of Training and Coaching with Performance Feedback on Teachers' Use of "Pyramid Model" Practices
citation: Mary Louise Hemmeter, Jessica K. Hardy, Alana G. Schnitz, Jessie Morris Adams, and Kiersten A. Kinder. (2015). Effects of Training and Coaching With Performance Feedback on Teachers' Use of Pyramid Model Practices. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121415594924
title: The Pyramid Model for Promoting Social-Emotional Competence in Young Children
description: The Pyramid Model is a comprehensive, tiered model for promoting young children's social-emotional development and addressing challenging behavior. "The Pyramid Model includes three tiers of support": universal practices for high-quality supportive environments and nurturing, responsive relationships; targeted social-emotional supports such as friendship skills, emotional literacy, anger management, and social problem-solving; and individualized tertiary interventions developed by a team with functional assessment. The article states effectiveness in inclusive settings depends on concurrent implementation across all tiers.
requirements: Ongoing training and coaching are needed for implementation with fidelity, per the implementation science framing the article cites
constraints: Effectiveness in inclusive settings depends on concurrent implementation of practices across all tiers, as the article states
target_learners: preschool children, including children with disabilities and children with persistent challenging behavior
target_learning_goals: prevention and reduction of challenging behavior
examples: Teachers in this study were coached on practices such as schedules and routines, behavior expectations, emotional literacy, and problem-solving drawn from the model's tiers
key_sources: Mary Louise Hemmeter, Jessica K. Hardy, Alana G. Schnitz, Jessie Morris Adams, and Kiersten A. Kinder. (2015). Effects of Training and Coaching With Performance Feedback on Teachers' Use of Pyramid Model Practices. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121415594924

article_title: Flipped classroom showdown: game-based vs. case-based learning in pharmacy education.
citation: Amini Mahtab, Amini Shahideh, Alizadeh Maryam. (2026). Flipped classroom showdown: game-based vs. case-based learning in pharmacy education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09754-y
title: Custom Python board game for hypertension pharmacotherapy with three difficulty levels
description: The GBL intervention was a board game format consisting of multiple-choice practical questions developed in Python 3.9, presenting questions randomly from a predefined question bank. Students could choose among three difficulty levels: Level 1 involved "the recollection of facts (Knowledge)", Level 2 "comprehending information (Comprehension)", and Level 3 "solving problems related to their clinical practice (Application & Analysis)". Questions and scenarios were standardized with input from three clinical pharmacy specialists.
requirements: Game design and standardization steps documented in Additional file 1; questions standardized with input from three clinical pharmacy specialists
constraints: The game was designed for this specific course, so comparison with other GBL interventions requires caution
target_learning_goals: hypertension pharmacotherapy knowledge and clinical application
examples: Participants played individually and in turn according to the game's rules for one hour in facilitated subgroups
key_sources: Amini Mahtab, Amini Shahideh, Alizadeh Maryam. (2026). Flipped classroom showdown: game-based vs. case-based learning in pharmacy education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09754-y

article_title: Artificial intelligence in medical ethics education: a descriptive study of eight models in multiple choice question generation.
citation: Obeid John, Bobier Christopher, Gillham Alex, Omelianchuk Adam, Hurst Daniel. (2026). Artificial intelligence in medical ethics education: a descriptive study of eight models in multiple choice question generation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08781-z
title: Automated Python API pipeline for consistent AI MCQ generation across models
description: The authors developed a Python script using Microsoft Visual Studio Code to automate data collection: it retrieved each learning objective from a spreadsheet, executed API calls to the language models, and stored responses in text files. A retry mechanism with a default 2-second delay reattempted failed API calls, and infinite loops with if/else statements handled error messages. The authors state the automated methodology ensures consistency in question formatting and phrasing while minimizing biases and errors associated with manual input.
requirements: Identical prompts across models; a retry mechanism with delay interval to handle errors and empty responses from API calls
constraints: A potential bias remained: reviewers knew the name of the AI model whose generated MCQs they were assessing, which the authors say may have affected ratings
target_learning_goals: Generation of USMLE-aligned medical ethics MCQs with consistent formatting
examples: The script produced 26 questions per model across 13 USMLE STEP 2 ethics learning objectives, 208 questions overall, using the identical professor-role prompt.
key_sources: Obeid John, Bobier Christopher, Gillham Alex, Omelianchuk Adam, Hurst Daniel. (2026). Artificial intelligence in medical ethics education: a descriptive study of eight models in multiple choice question generation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08781-z
